opus-5.5.text:
I think about it very much as a partnership. For a long time the way we've approached prosthetics is as a tool: the person sends a command, through a muscle signal or a switch, and the device does exactly that thing and nothing more. All the intelligence, all the adaptation, sits on the human side. The person has to learn the device, and the device never learns the person.

What becomes possible when we bring machine learning, and especially reinforcement learning and continual prediction, into the limb is that both sides start adapting to each other. The device can learn to anticipate what the person is likely to do next. It can predict which joint they'll want to move, how a grasp is going to unfold, what the next few hundred milliseconds of their intent probably look like. And it can use those predictions to make control smoother, to switch between functions at the right moment, or to give the person feedback about what it expects.

So I like to frame it as communicative capital. Over time, the person and the machine build up a shared history, a kind of trust and mutual understanding, in the same way you build that with a colleague or a partner on a sports team. In the early days the interaction is clunky and explicit. Later it becomes fluid, almost tacit. The person stops thinking about the arm and starts thinking about the task.

That also raises questions we take seriously. How much agency should the device have? When should it act on its predictions versus wait to be told? How do we keep the person firmly in charge while still letting the machine carry some of the load? For me the goal isn't an autonomous robot bolted onto someone's body. It's a device that becomes part of the person's own extended self, something that amplifies their intentions rather than replacing them. The best outcome is when someone forgets where they stop and the technology begins, because the two have learned to work together so well.

r001.rationale: The response describes a partnership in which the person and device adapt to each other and build mutual understanding, clearly framing them as interacting agents.

r002.rationale: The response says machine learning and continual prediction enable the limb to learn and anticipate, but it does not identify increased computational capacity as what makes treating the limb as an agent possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that it's really a relationship, not a tool and a user. When someone puts on a prosthetic arm that has some learning capacity built into it, you now have two agents sharing a body. One is the person, who has goals, who wants to pick up a coffee cup or button a shirt. The other is the device, which is sensing, predicting, and adapting in real time. Neither one can do the job alone.

So the question I keep coming back to is: how do those two learn about each other? A conventional prosthesis is static. The person does all the adapting, and that's exhausting. People abandon these devices because the burden of control is too high. What we try to do is let the limb carry some of that load. It watches the signals coming from the muscles, it watches what the person tends to do next, and it starts making predictions. Over time it can anticipate, and the control gets smoother because the device is meeting the person partway.

But I'd stress that it has to be a two-way street. The person needs to be able to teach the device, correct it, and understand roughly why it did what it did. If the limb is a black box that occasionally surprises you, you won't trust it, and trust is everything when something is literally attached to your body. So we think a lot about communication, about the device giving feedback and the person giving feedback, and about keeping the human firmly in charge of the goals while the machine helps with the mechanics.

I sometimes describe it as a partnership. The best version of this isn't a limb that replaces what was lost. It's a limb that grows with the person, learns their habits, and becomes something they experience as part of themselves rather than as equipment they operate.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes the person and prosthetic device as “two agents sharing a body” and calls their relationship a partnership.

r002.rationale: The response says the limb has learning capacity and can sense, predict, and adapt, but it does not identify increased computational capacity as what makes treating the limb as an agent possible.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as a partnership. The person is learning how to use the artificial limb, and the limb should also be learning how to work with that person. It shouldn’t all fall on the human to adapt to a fixed piece of technology.

That makes the relationship something that develops over time. The system can learn from the person’s movements and feedback, while the person learns what the system can do and when they can trust it. The goal is for those two learning processes to support each other, so that together they can do more than either could alone.

And the person’s goals have to guide that partnership. It’s not simply about making a limb more autonomous. It’s about giving someone more ability to act in the world, with less effort spent managing the technology.

r001.rationale: The response describes the person and limb as partners, each learning from the other, with their learning processes supporting each other—clearly framing them as multiple interacting agents.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention increased computational capacity or say that it makes treating the limb as an agent possible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a partnership. The person is learning how to use the limb, but the limb should also be learning how to work with the person. It’s a relationship that develops through interaction, rather than something we configure once and then consider finished.

An artificial limb is especially interesting because it’s so closely coupled to the person. What the person does changes the signals the limb receives, and what the limb does changes how the person responds. So we need to think about that whole loop: how they learn together, how they communicate, and how the person can guide that learning.

The goal isn’t simply to make the limb more autonomous. It’s to make it a more useful partner—one that reduces the effort required to do what the person wants, while keeping the person in control.

r001.rationale: The response describes the person and limb as partners that learn and affect each other through interaction, framing their relationship as involving two active participants.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention increased computational capacity or say that it makes treating the limb as an agent possible.
